data.title: Danuvina Alacris – a Roman patrol boat back on the Danube
data.excerpt: The story of Danuvina Alacris, a fully functional replica of a 4th-century Roman patrol boat, began in 2020 as one of the main outputs of the Living Danube Limes project. In April 2024 the vessel returned to the water at Krems an der Donau and a crew of twenty rowers took her down the Danube to Tulln, the site of the Roman fort of Comagena.
data.metaTitle: Danuvina Alacris – a Roman boat back on the Danube
data.metaDescription: Danuvina Alacris, a replica of a 4th-century Roman patrol boat built for the Living Danube Limes project, is rowing the Danube again from Krems to Tulln.

mediaTexts.alt: A replica of a Roman river boat with a swan figurehead on the bow, moored at a jetty

children.text: The story of the replica of the Roman rowing boat named Danuvina Alacris began in 2020. This beautiful vessel is one of the main outputs of the “Living Danube Limes” project. Preparations for building a fully functional reconstruction of a 4th-century patrol boat began in June 2020 under the “main command” of Prof. Boris Dreyer of the Friedrich Alexander University of Erlangen and Nuremberg. What did these Roman ships, or rather boats, in which the Romans advanced deep into this territory and later patrolled the river frontiers, actually look like? What were they made of? What technology was used to propel them? What speeds could they reach and what distances could they cover? Who were the rowers? Answers to some of these questions have already been found, but what was it like in real life? Prof. Dr. Boris Dreyer,
a specialist in ancient history
, has been exploring these questions in a very unusual way since 2016, when he began reconstructing and testing Roman river boats.
Preparations began with photographing and measuring the wreck of a Roman patrol boat in the Museum of Ancient Seafaring (
Ger
. Museum für antike Schifffahrt), which was installed in
Mainz
in 1994 in the former central covered market hall as a branch of the Roman-Germanic Central Museum in Mainz.

blocks.alt: DANUVINA ALACRIS back on the waters of the Danube

children.text: Oak and larch timber from the Bavarian Forest was chosen as the wood suitable for building the reconstruction of the boat. Construction of the new vessel named Danuvina Alacris began with the laying of the keel in May 2021.

Even all the tools used to build the boat – axes, hammers, chisels and nails – were hand-forged and made using period techniques based on archaeological finds. The axe, for example, was made after an axe found in the Roman legionary camp in the province of Germania Inferior – VETERA CASTRA. Vetera was one of the most important garrisons on the northern wing of the Roman Empire and in its early days it was an important base for Roman expansion on the right bank of the Rhine. There are two camps here – the younger Vetera I, from the period 13/12 BC to AD 70, and the older one, called Vetera II, from the period from AD 71 to about the 3rd century. These two forts lie about 1,500 m apart. Today Vetera I lies in undeveloped land within the municipal area of Xanten, while Vetera II is now as much as 10 metres below the surface of a lake formed in a quarry. The replica of the rowing boat, which was given the name Danuvina Alacris (from the Latin for “the nimble Danubian”), sailed from Germany – from Ingolstadt to Romania – in 2022 and covered about 2,400 km along the Danube. The Danube and the Danube limes play a central role in the project. The Danube stretches across Europe as its second longest river. It is about 2,850 km long, rises in the Black Forest in Germany and flows into the Black Sea on the border between Romania and Ukraine. The Danube passes through ten countries and often forms state borders. Already in Roman times the Danube served along almost its entire length as the frontier between the Roman Empire to the south and Barbaricum to the north.

blocks.alt: DANUVINA ALACRIS back on the waters of the Danube

children.text: In 2022 we brought you a two-part article about the voyage on the Danuvina Alacris during the 4th stage, on the Budapest – Baja (HU) section – you will find it here:
/hladat?q=danuvina+alacris

. On 18 April 2024 this unique vessel returned to the water of the Danube after a long time, in the town of Krems an der Donau. Krems is one of the oldest habitats on the Danube. A charter has survived from the year 995 which mentions a fortress called “Chremisa”. This makes Krems the oldest town in Lower Austria. The area was, however, already occupied in the Palaeolithic, as is shown by the “Venus of Galgenberg” (a figurine of a woman more than 32,000 years old). The original of this delicate figure is displayed in the Natural History Museum together with the Venus of Willendorf, which is several thousand years younger.
After the Romans, around AD 480, the Germanic Rugii settled in Stein. The Romans, who always had a taste for the finer things, cultivated vines in the surroundings of Krems.

blocks.alt: DANUVINA ALACRIS back on the waters of the Danube

children.text: This legacy from Roman times pleases our eyes, nose and palate all along the Danube route: wine. Wine was already grown throughout the Danube valley in Roman times. Grape cultivation was very successful in the Wachau and the Vienna Basin, which are still regarded as classic locations today. Roman wine growers probably laid the foundations of the viticulture from which the local varieties later emerged. Krems-Stein was the most important transhipment point between water and land transport, even more important than Vienna was at the time.
After an inspection and the necessary minor repairs, some of the rowers, the captain, some of the builders and even Prof. Boris Dreyer returned aboard the Danuvina Alacris.

The boat set out from the Austrian town of Krems an der Donau in the early morning of 19 April 2024. At 9.30 a.m. it was quite chilly in the cargo port at Krems an der Donau, only around 6 to 7 °C, which left us all frozen through, but not even this weather could put us off. The crew consisted of 20 rowers, the captain and the “fleet commander”, Prof. Dreyer. Most of the crew members knew one another from two years earlier, so it was a cheerful and pleasant reunion.

blocks.alt: DANUVINA ALACRIS back on the waters of the Danube

children.text: After rowing about 16 km we reached the Altenwörth lock around lunchtime; it lies at kilometre 1,979.8 of the Danube. This lock is one of the highest in Austria and was built in 1978. Passing through this lock was a powerful experience for every one of us. Once out of the dam complex, another 15 km of rowing to the town of Tulln lay ahead of us. For safety reasons we all had to put on life jackets on this stretch, which looked rather comical over our tunics. In the 1st century AD Roman troops were stationed along the Danube. Armed horsemen controlled what was then the northern frontier of the Roman Empire. In this period fortifications were built that offered protection. The Romans also chose the area of today’s town of Tulln as the right place to build such a fortification. Comagena grew up on this spot. This also laid the foundations of present-day Tulln – a town with 2,000 years of history.

blocks.alt: DANUVINA ALACRIS back on the waters of the Danube

children.text: Tulln, too, is one of the oldest towns in Austria, precisely because of its position right on the bank of the Danube. The Romans already regarded this as a clear advantage: Comagena, or Comagenis, was a Roman cavalry fort (an Alenkastell for 500 horsemen) on the “Noric Limes” in the territory of present-day Austria. The area of the former cavalry fort extended over what is today the Marcus Aurelius Park, and the northern part of the camp was in time completely eaten away by the Danube. Since 2021 the archaeological monument has been part of the Danube limes, which is inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site.

The exceptional strategic importance of the fort follows from its exposed position. Its garrison controlled a militarily important ford across the Danube and monitored the Tullnerfeld, which was clearly visible from here. The fort was built at the end of the 1st century, probably under the emperor Domitian, as a timber-and-earth fort, and at the beginning of the 2nd century it was enlarged into a stone fort. Several phases of rebuilding are known from the beginning of its occupation until the end of the 5th century. From late antiquity Comagena was also a base of the Danube fleet and the seat of a cavalry unit. To the west and south of the fort, excavations have revealed the presence of at least two civilian settlements (vicus) and three cemeteries. The destruction of the fort around AD 400 was followed by a phase of civilian occupation lasting until the end of antiquity, with renewed occupation at the beginning of the 8th century.

blocks.alt: DANUVINA ALACRIS back on the waters of the Danube

children.text: The Danuvina Alacris remains moored in the town of Tulln. In August 2024 she is to be taken for a short time to the Czech Republic, where visitors to the “Gateway to the Roman Empire” near Mušov are waiting for her. In the autumn she should be brought back to Tulln. She will leave the port of Tulln on 10 October 2024 and set out on a voyage to Bratislava, where we shall probably be able to welcome her again on 13 October 2024.
As a matter of interest, we also add the basic technical data of the Danuvina Alacris:
18 m — length
2.8 m — beam at the widest point
5–6 tonnes — unladen weight
20 rowers
built exclusively using Gallo-Roman shipbuilding methods.
